Chapter 10: The Cost to Society
When you think about the struggles of low-wage workers, it’s easy to picture just one person—maybe someone you see every day. But the truth is, these challenges don't stop with individuals. They ripple out, affecting families, neighborhoods, and even the entire country.
Imagine this: if people can’t afford decent housing, neighborhoods start to decline. If parents are forced to juggle multiple jobs just to scrape by, their kids often end up without the support and guidance they need. And when someone’s feeling sick but can’t afford to see a doctor, it’s not just their health on the line—public health takes a hit, too.
Picture a teacher who’s noticed more and more students coming to school hungry or exhausted. She does what she can—maybe bringing snacks from home, offering a kind word, or just listening. But deep down, she knows her efforts aren’t enough. The problems her students face are bigger than anything she can solve by herself.
Employers feel these effects, too. High turnover, low morale, and lost productivity—these are the hidden costs that come with low wages and tough working conditions. Sure, cutting costs may seem to help businesses in the short term, but the long-term damage is real. Communities start to fall apart, trust fades, and hope can slowly disappear.
Most folks don’t see these connections. They don’t realize how poverty isn’t just a personal struggle—it’s a challenge for all of us. And when we ignore it, everyone pays the price, in ways that are both obvious and sometimes completely invisible.
